strengths: Addresses a real practical problem: provides a feasible alternative to the theoretically optimal but practically infeasible MASTER algorithm
Order-optimal theoretical guarantees with clean, modular regret bound that applies to multiple parametric bandit variants (PS-LB, PS-GLB, PS-SCB)
Significant empirical improvements over state-of-the-art methods (MASTER, ADA-OPKB, WeightUCB) across multiple settings and change frequencies
Black-box modularity is valuable: works with any stationary bandit algorithm and preserves its regret properties
Unexpectedly strong performance in drifting environments with intuitive explanation and supporting experiments (Section 5.2)

Comprehensive experiments with multiple bandit variants, noise levels, and change-point frequencies, with error bars over 30 runs

strengths: Practical black-box framework effectively addresses limitations of prior work (MASTER) with solid engineering and modularity

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple bandit settings (PS-LB, PS-GLB, PS-SCB, PS-KB) with both synthetic and real-world benchmarks showing consistent improvements
Practical black-box framework with genuine modularity—applicable to any stationary bandit algorithm with no algorithm-specific modifications needed
Honest acknowledgment of limitations including restrictive change-point spacing assumptions and lack of theoretical guarantees for drifting environments
Broad applicability to both parametric and non-parametric bandit variants, extending beyond prior work that focused on specific settings

strengths: Strong practical framework design: Black-box modular approach that accepts any stationary bandit algorithm and augments it with change detection is elegant and broadly applicable

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive experiments across 4 bandit variants (PB and NPB), synthetic benchmarks, and 6 real-world datasets demonstrate consistent outperformance of multiple strong baselines

Improved theoretical bounds: Matches state-of-the-art for PS-LBs/PS-GLBs and improves best known bounds for PS-SCBs (to O(d√N_T T) vs. prior O(d^{2/3}T^{2/3}N_T^{1/3})) and PS-KBs (to O(√γ_T N_T T) vs. O(√dγ_T N_T T))
Well-motivated problem setting: Justifies focus on piecewise stationarity as practically relevant and demonstrates PS algorithms can extend to drifting scenarios
Clear and insightful presentation: Intuitive explanations (e.g., Section 4.3 on drifting environments) make the work accessible while maintaining technical rigor

weaknesses: Restrictive theoretical assumptions: The required separation condition ν_k - ν_{k-1} ≥ Õ(√T/k) is violated in experiments (e.g., ξ=0.4 produces frequent changes), creating a gap between theory and practice that limits theoretical guarantees' relevance

Limited fundamental technical novelty: Core contributions (GLR test from [7,27], forced exploration, stationary algorithm wrapping) are from existing work; Theorem 4.3 is largely a direct application of [27] with parameter substitution. Main novelty is adaptation rather than innovation

Incomplete drifting analysis: Section 4.3 provides only intuitive explanations without formal guarantees. The random walk experiment (Figure 3) is limited to d=5 linear bandits. Lacks theoretical characterization of when DAL succeeds under drift or how drift rate δ impacts detectability

Practical tuning and feasibility gaps: Covering set construction requires domain knowledge (linearly independent actions in Proposition 4.1, Lipschitz constants in 4.2). 'Prior-free' claim is weakened by hidden parameters

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation with extensive real-world benchmarks and novel microarchitecture dataset, first to rigorously evaluate order-optimal baselines on real data
Practical black-box framework that accepts any stationary bandit algorithm with principled hyperparameter selection, attractive for practitioners

Clear algorithm design and honest discussion of limitations including theory-practice gaps and drifting environment challenges

weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: core contribution is extending [31]'s approach to general bandits; GLR detector, detection-based restarts, and covering set constructions are standard techniques

Incomplete drifting environment analysis: Section 4.3 provides only empirical analysis and informal hypothesis; lacks regret bounds and rigorous justification for observed performance advantages

Experimental setup concerns: asymmetric hyperparameter tuning (ADA-OPKB: 7 hyperparameters vs DAL: theory-derived), varying covering set construction, missing confidence intervals in Figure 2, and unclear fairness in baseline comparisons

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: First thorough validation of non-stationary bandits across multiple variants (LBs, GLBs, SCBs, KBs, CBs) in both piecewise-stationary and drifting settings, including 9 diverse real-world datasets
Practical modular framework: Black-box design allows any stationary algorithm to be augmented for non-stationarity, with genuine applicability for practitioners
Sound theoretical contributions: Regret bounds match state-of-the-art in PS-LBs/GLBs/CBs and improve bounds for PS-SCBs and PS-KBs (removes √d factor in KB case)
Breadth of applicability: Extends detection-based approaches beyond MABs to general bandit settings, providing first order-optimal baseline empirical study
Novel dataset contribution: Microarchitecture prefetcher selection benchmark from SPEC06/17 for reproducible real-world evaluation
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: GLR detector and restart-based framework directly adapted from Huang et al. [31]; main contribution is mechanical application to general bandits rather than fundamental innovation

Misleading 'prior-free' claims: Covering set construction requires structural assumptions (linear independence in NS-PBs, existence of appreciable mean-shift action in NS-KBs) that constitute substantial prior knowledge; for unstructured NS-CBs, must explore all actions

Inadequate drifting environment analysis: Section 4.3 provides only post-hoc explanation without theoretical guarantees; Figure 3 shows DAL significantly underperforms WeightUCB for large drift rates—a critical limitation discussed in ~2 paragraphs

Restrictive change-point separation assumption: Theory requires ν_k - ν_{k-1} = Õ(√T/k); authors claim experiments violate this but use geometric distributions that naturally provide separation, making claim misleading
Covering set exponential in dimension: For NS-KBs, N_e ≤ ⌈√(dR/2δ_T)⌉^d scales exponentially; experiments work around by setting A_e = A (all actions), introducing substantial exploration overhead
Incremental regret improvements: PS-SCB improvement compares prior-free vs prior-based methods; PS-KB improvement is algorithm-specific and modest relative to prior-free baseline ADA-OPKB

strengths: Comprehensive real-world empirical evaluation: First systematic evaluation of order-optimal non-stationary bandit methods (MASTER, ADA-OPKB) across 9 diverse real-world datasets spanning click logs, finance, clinical trials, microarchitecture, and sensors—filling a significant gap where prior work focused almost exclusively on synthetic data

Meaningful theoretical improvements: Improved regret bounds for PS-SCBs (from Õ(d^{2/3}T^{2/3}N_T^{1/3}) to Õ(d√(N_T T))) and PS-KBs (from Õ(√d γ_T N_T T) to Õ(√γ_T N_T T)), with novel analysis extending detection-based methods to general bandit settings

Genuinely modular black-box design: Framework accepts any stationary algorithm as input with only three components (detector, exploration scheme, algorithm), simplifying non-stationary algorithm design
Consistent empirical performance: DAL outperforms prior-free baselines (MASTER, ADA-OPKB, ADA-ILTCB+) and competitive prior-based methods across all tested settings and variants

Honest treatment of limitations: Transparent discussion of gap between theory (change-point separation assumption) and practice (experiments violate assumption without degradation), with empirical investigation of drifting regime performance
Novel real-world benchmark: Microarchitecture prefetcher dataset based on SPEC06/17 benchmarks provides new testbed for community evaluation
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with intuitive algorithm description and three-component decomposition clearly explained
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: GLR detector from [31], forced exploration well-established; main contribution is combination and extension to general bandits with evaluation, which is somewhat incremental

Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.4 requires change-point separation ν_k - ν_{k-1} = Õ(√(T/k)), but experiments deliberately violate this (ξ ∈ {0.4,0.6,0.8}); explanation in Remark 4.6 is intuitive but non-rigorous with no formal regret bound for missed short intervals

Incomplete analysis of drifting regime: Section 4.3 provides only empirical hypothesis without formal regret guarantees; phase transition in Figure 3 (δ critical threshold) is observed but not theoretically characterized; claims good performance on drifting but only tested on one linear drift model in LBs

Modest empirical improvements: While consistent, improvements over baselines are often small (Figures 1-2); in many cases differences are within reasonable noise margins, limiting practical significance

Synthetic non-stationarity in real datasets: Real-world benchmarks impose artificial change-points on stock data and add synthetic shifts to parameter vectors rather than using naturally non-stationary sequences, limiting conclusions about real-world benefit

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Limited comparison with closely related NS-MAB detection methods from [7,9,31]; for NS-CBs only compares two baselines without covering other prior-free detection methods

Misleading 'hyperparameter-free' claim: DAL has hyperparameters (α_k, δ_F, δ_D, covering set construction, exploration frequency); while fewer than some baselines, claiming 'hyperparameter-free' is inaccurate

Remark 3.1 modification weakens black-box claim: Critical deviation where change-detection on actions outside A_e substantially changes algorithm behavior from theory, but stated to 'not affect theoretical properties'—this is not rigorously justified
Missing statistical significance analysis: Figures 1-2 lack error bars despite only 15 trials; unclear if improvements are statistically significant in all cases

strengths: Practical black-box framework addressing genuine need for handling piecewise stationarity without prior knowledge, with demonstrated applicability across diverse bandit variants
Novel 'detect-the-model' paradigm using change detection on covering sets, fundamentally different from prior work (e.g., MASTER) and empirically effective

Comprehensive experimental validation: 5 bandit types, 9 datasets (including first real-world evaluation of order-optimal non-stationary baselines), consistent improvements over MASTER/ADA-OPKB/ADA-ILTCB+, and competitive runtime
Theoretical contributions including Theorem 4.8 that matches or improves state-of-the-art regret bounds (improved bounds for PS-SCBs and PS-KBs)
Clear characterization of covering set construction for parametric and kernelized bandits (Propositions 4.2-4.3) with efficient preprocessing
Insight into why detection-based approach works for slowly drifting environments (Section 4.3), bridging gap between piecewise stationary and continuous drift regimes
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Assumption 4.6 requires change-point separation O(√T/k), emerging from conservative proof technique, while experiments violate it without apparent harm—justification in Remark 4.7 is informal

Covering set construction has practical limitations: requires d linearly independent actions for PBs (may not exist in finite spaces), assumes verifiable mean-shift condition for KBs (Prop 4.3), and requires Ae=A for CBs (limits scalability)

Limited theoretical novelty: core detection mechanism (GLR/GSR) and analysis framework from Huang et al. (2025), with main contributions being application to general bandits and covering set constructions

Drifting environment analysis only empirical without formal regret guarantees; condition that drift absorbed into noise when δ small lacks formalization; Figure 4 shows WeightUCB outperforms DAL for large δ

Gap between claimed hyperparameter-freedom and actual requirements: δT selection needed for KBs, exploration frequency αk from theory may require tuning, unlike MASTER comparison

strengths: Strong empirical contribution: First comprehensive real-world evaluation of order-optimal non-stationary bandits across 9 diverse datasets with consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines
Clean black-box framework that combines any order-optimal stationary algorithm with change detection, providing modularity and generality across multiple bandit variants
Novel 'detect-the-model' paradigm is conceptually cleaner than detecting regret bound violations and demonstrates superior empirical performance compared to MASTER
Technically sound with complete regret analysis (Theorem 4.8, Corollary 4.9) and formal characterization of required detector properties (Property 4.1)
Practical feasibility demonstrated: makes theoretically order-optimal methods computationally practical (unlike MASTER requiring 143B horizon)
Comprehensive experimental details with multiple datasets, runtime analysis, and plan to release microarchitecture benchmark dataset
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Assumption 4.6 requiring Õ(√(T/k)) change-point separation is violated in experiments (ξ=0.4) yet theory claims optimality only under this assumption. Incomplete drifting analysis: Section 4.3 presents speculative hypothesis about drift absorption without theoretical guarantees. Paper explicitly acknowledges 'regret guarantees for detection-based methods in drifting environments remain unexplored,' yet includes empirical section suggesting completion

strengths: Addresses critical practical gap: First practical prior-free black-box method for general PS bandits; MASTER is theoretically optimal but impractical (requires 143B horizon)

Clean modular framework: Algorithm 1 is implementable and separates detection, exploration, and bandit algorithm; enables flexibility in component choices
Sound theoretical framework: Property 4.1 clearly identifies detector requirements; Propositions 4.2-4.3 provide principled Ae constructions; Theorem 4.8 carefully decomposes regret
Well-presented with reproducibility: Clear writing, informative figures, detailed algorithms, comprehensive appendix; most datasets public; hyperparameters specified

weaknesses: Conservative change-point separation assumption: Assumption 4.6 requires νk − νk−1 ≥ Õ(√T/k), limiting applicability to moderate change rates; empirical validation that violations don't degrade performance lacks formal justification

Limited theoretical novelty: Detectors (GLR/GSR) are from recent work; restart framework is standard; for PS-PBs/KBs, proof closely follows Huang et al. (2025) with minor substitutions; main contribution is integration and PS-CB analysis, which is incremental

Covering set construction gaps: Proposition 4.3 requires knowledge of reference point ã with appreciable changes; somewhat circular—must know where changes occur to design Ae for detecting them; reduces transparency

Insufficient drifting analysis: Figure 4 shows crossover with WeightUCB at δ≈0.16; no detailed analysis of this transition or how practitioners should select δ
Limited detection diagnostics: No empirical analysis of false alarm/missed detection rates; practitioners lack understanding of restart frequency for tuning parameters
Micro-prefetcher dataset not yet released: Promised for release but not currently available, limiting reproducibility of novel benchmark
